summary: The Independent explains that UK clocks go back one hour at 2am on Sunday 29 October 2023 and forward again on Sunday 31 March 2024, then lays out expert arguments over abolishing Daylight Saving Time. Proponents cite energy savings, fewer road accidents, better sleep and fewer depressive episodes, while one author points to a drop in heart attacks after the autumn change. It also covers the 1916 origin of British Summer Time and the stalled 2019 European parliament vote to scrap DST.
one_line: Explains the October 2023 UK clock change and weighs expert arguments for and against abolishing Daylight Saving Time, from energy savings to health and safety.
key_facts: UK clocks go back one hour at 2am on Sunday 29 October 2023 and do not go forward again until Sunday 31 March 2024.
Professor Aoife Foley of Queen's University Belfast calculated households could save more than £400 per year on electricity, depending on tariff, if DST were scrapped at the end of October.
Dr Foley estimates a saving of £1.20 a day and says dropping winter DST would reduce demand on the National Grid.
Winter evening energy demand peaks between 5pm and 7pm, and the National Grid warned UK households could face three-hour power cuts due to a gas shortage.
The Royal Society for the Prevention of Accidents (RoSPA) calls for the government to adopt British Summer Time (GMT+1) all year to avoid sudden autumn darkness on commutes.
Figures from the RAC Foundation state road traffic collisions rise 19 per cent in the fortnight after clocks go back, and fall 11 per cent when clocks go forward.
Giulia Guerrini of Medino advises seven to eight hours of sleep consistently and says a one-hour clock shift can throw the circadian rhythm off balance.
Sleep School told The Independent it is 'impartial' on how clock changes affect sleep, stressing sleep duration and a consistent schedule.

A 2017 Danish study of more than 185,000 people over 15 years found an 11 per cent rise in depressive episodes after the switch from summer time to standard time, with no effect from the switch to summer time.
Charlie Morley cites a 2014 College of Cardiology study and claims a 21 per cent decrease in heart attacks the day after clocks go back, affecting 1.6 billion people in 70 countries.
The UK first introduced Daylight Saving Time in 1916 with British Summer Time (BST) to encourage more time outdoors in daylight.
The European parliament voted to scrap DST in 2019, with the change due in 2021, but plans have stalled.
A 2019 YouGov poll found 44 per cent of Brits wanted to keep the current system while 39 per cent favoured ditching the change.
